question: How do Japanese housemakers build prefabricated houses that are both high quality and economical?

answer.answer:
Standardise the components first (AT7, drawn on by 25 of the 50 coded cases) and run them at industrialised scale (AT8, 23), because industrialised production is the strongest cited route to improved quality/performance (VA3) and it rests on standardisation, on vertical integration (CO10) and on an adapted delivery and business model (RI12); moving the work off site (PR2) then adds quality again plus reduced errors and rework (VA10) and better site safety (VA13). Economy in this record is mostly indirect, through reduced time and productivity gains (VA2) and reduced construction complexity (VA7): the single cited dependency edge touching Reduce cost (VA6) runs from robotic assembly (PR4) and is carried by 7 of the 50, so cost is not something the literature connects to prefabrication directly. Watch the price of the standardisation route: reliance on precise planning (RI14) is carried by 18 of the 50 cases that prefabricate, design compromise from over-standardisation (RI15) and production and assembly restriction (RI19) are drawn on by 17 and 25 of the 50 with no cited edge to explain them, and the claim that standardisation lets you accommodate late design changes (VA21) is carried by only 2 cases. Note that the deployed side of this answer is thin: eleven cases sit at the housemaker stakeholder tier but the material in front of me gives them as ids only, and the terms "Japanese housemakers" and "houses" are not ones the record itself carries.

**The quality route**

Two distinct cited paths lead to Improve quality/performance (VA3), which 37 of the 50 coded cases draw on. The first runs through industrialisation: Industrialised (AT8) enables Improve quality/performance (VA3), on the finding that quality-oriented industrialised production considerably increases housing quality by providing standard fittings [1], peer-reviewed evidence, and that edge is carried by 22 of the 50 coded cases [2], the most heavily exhibited edge into VA3 here. The second runs through the factory itself: Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enables Improve quality/performance (VA3) because a controlled factory environment improves quality [3], carried by 18 of the 50 [2]. Off-site work also reduces errors and rework through factory-based quality control (VA10) [4], carried by 14 of the 50 [2], and improves site safety (VA13) by moving work off site [5], carried by 12 of the 50 [2].

**What industrialisation requires upstream**

Read the relations, not the arrows. AT8 dependsOn AT7 "Highly standardised", carried by 16 of the 50 [2], so standardisation is the requirement and comes first in practice. AT8 also dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", carried by 13 of the 50: adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [2]. Coming the other way, CO10 "Vertical integration" enablesCapability AT8, carried by 17 of the 50, on mirror-breaking vertical integration enabling digital manufacturing at industrialised scale [2], and CO4 "DFAB digital twin" enables AT8 too, but that edge is carried by just 1 of the 50 [2]. Of AT8's own cited preconditions, then, one is an attribute of the product, one is an organisational condition and one is a risk about business model: none is a machine.

Standardisation itself pays out widely. AT7 carries six outbound edges: it enables Configurators/kit-of-parts (AR6), carried by 11 of the 50 [2], DfMA for DFAB process (PR9), 13 [2], Modular (AT2), 11 [2], Reduce construction complexity (VA7), 15 [2], Robotic assembly (PR4), 10, on Japanese automated erection systems relying on standardised prefabricated components [2] [6], and Accommodate late design changes (VA21), carried by only 2 [2]. That last asymmetry matters: VA21 is drawn on by 3 of the 50 [2] against 15 for VA7 [2], so the flexibility argument for standardised interfaces is asserted in the literature and barely exhibited, while the complexity-reduction argument is well carried.

**The economy route**

Reduce cost (VA6) is drawn on by 22 of the 50 coded cases [2] and carries 1 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges [2], which is an exact count: that one edge is PR4 "Robotic assembly" amplifies VA6, carried by 7 of the 50 [2]. Nothing cited connects prefabrication, standardisation or industrialisation to cost directly. What they do connect to is time: PR2 enables VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" because off-site work compresses schedule, carried by 19 of the 50 [2], PR4 amplifies VA2, carried by 13 [2], and VA2 is drawn on by 49 of the 50 coded cases [2], the most widely drawn-on enabler in this set. Alongside that sit the loss-avoidance values, VA10 at 19 of the 50 [2] and VA7 at 16 [2]. Two further levers bear on investment risk: VA9 "Allow traceable/linked data" mitigates RI3 "Increase cost/investment uncertainty", carried by 7 of the 50 [2], and CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" enables VA10 through tolerance verification, carried by 9 [2].

**Robotic assembly, if you go that far**

Robotic assembly (PR4) is drawn on by 13 of the 50 [2]. Its cited preconditions are uneven. PR4 dependsOn RE2 "Robotic arm", carried by 12 of the 50 [2], and PR4 hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", on the finding that automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [7], carried by 4 of the 50 [2]. Two more direct preconditions are cited in the literature and carried by almost nobody: PR12 "Path-planning" enables PR4, carried by 2 of the 50, although 26 cases draw on PR12 in its own right [2], and CO12 "Mobile factory" (a Condition, not a machine) enables PR4 on the all-weather-cover mechanism, carried by 0 of the 50 [2]. CO12 itself is drawn on by 1 of the 50 [2], and it is also the precondition for On-site DFAB (PR8), environments needing to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over [8], that edge carried by 1 case [2]. In short, of PR4's cited requirements the robot arm is carried by 12 of the 50 and the enclosed mobile factory by none.

**What to watch**

PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning", carried by 18 of the 50: prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [2], and 36 of the 50 cases draw on RI14 [2], making it one of the most pervasive exposures in the record. PR2 also dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", carried by 10 of the 50, where compliance for off-site work requires third-party certification and traceability [2]. Three further risks bear directly on the standardise-and-industrialise strategy and the literature has connected none of them: RI19 "Production/assembly restriction" is drawn on by 25 of the 50 and carries no dependency edges [2], RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" by 17, also edgeless [2], and RI1 "Increase uncertainty in production" by 14, edgeless [2]. An enabler with no edge is present and usable: the evidence for it is how many of the 50 cases draw on it; it is simply not something the literature has connected yet. [2]

**The deployed record here**

Eleven cases carry the housemaker stakeholder tier: RP17, RP2, RP29, RP32, RP45, RP49, RP5, RP50, RP6, RP8 and RP9, and that is the complete set for that value. [9] The retrieved material gives these as identifiers only: it does not say what any of them built, which enablers each draws on, or which firm stands behind them, so I cannot rest any of the above on a named deployed project. On the census side, the only link retrieved is material: steel (Material_Steel) is used by a long list of census deployments including census_RXH1-1, census_RXH5-1, census_RXI2-1 and census_RXM6-6, with no further description attached. Treat the quality and economy findings above as literature-cited edges with case-carried counts, not as accounts of particular projects.
